biography.plain_text: Craig McCaw is an American telecommunications entrepreneur who built on a cable business transferred by his father to him and his brothers. He expanded it into a cellular empire later sold to AT&T. Based in Washington state, he subsequently backed communications ventures through Eagle River and helped develop wireless broadband provider Clearwire.

confidence.reason: The detailed transfer account, wireless history and official investment profiles support the family platform, expansion, sale and subsequent ventures. No disputed acquisition price or inferred current portfolio weighting appears.

long_biography.plain_text:
Craig McCaw helped make cellular service national by assembling local licences and networks that had developed as separate markets. When regulators awarded new licences by lottery, he bought rights from winners and combined them with existing operations. Partnerships with other carriers extended the reach of the Cellular One name. He recruited experienced executives to organise the businesses he acquired into a more coherent service.

He also applied his interest in communications to economic development. With Susan McCaw, he financed Grameen Foundation’s effort to adapt Bangladesh’s village-phone programme for other countries. That partnership grew into the Grameen Technology Center, which explored how communications technology could help people on low incomes. Its work included giving farmers and expectant mothers useful information by mobile phone and helping people establish small businesses.

Family transfer is not a euphemism for an independent start. The detailed 2000 Forbes account states ownership had already been transferred to the sons before the father's death; older Forbes and AP accounts use inheritance shorthand. The former gives the more specific legal sequence. Personal operating expansion was substantial, but the transferred cable asset and its proceeds financed the later fortune.

Current Forbes biography gives a 1994 sale and a different headline price from older accounts; some profiles conflate announcement, enterprise value and completion, and TNC gives 1996. Biographies therefore omit exact dates and prices. Corporate proceeds are never assigned wholly to Craig.

Present family members' holdings, former spouses' settlements and charitable-foundation assets are not included in his private portfolio. No family office is inferred merely from Eagle River ownership; sustained investment activity supports Investor.
